competitors.name: SignUpGenius
competitors.model: Freemium, ad-supported. Free tier serves banner + popup + video ads on the participant-facing sheet. Silver $11.99/mo ($107.89/yr annual) buys exactly ONE ad-free sign up; Gold $29.99/mo = 10 ad-free; Platinum $59.99/mo = unlimited ad-free. 5% + $0.50 on any money collected.
competitors.note: Owns the category by default — 'send a Genius' is a verb in PTAs and churches. Deep feature set (shifts, custom questions, payments, reminders). But it is the most-hated incumbent in its own reviews: iOS app sits at 1.2 stars / 125 ratings per the App Store listing. Charging over $100/yr to remove ads from a single volunteer sheet is the single biggest wedge in this market.

competitors.name: SignUp.com
competitors.model: Freemium. Free tier has ads, 1 organizer, 25 concurrent active tasks. Starter $8.34/mo, Plus $20.83/mo, Max $41.66/mo, Campus $99/yr.
competitors.note: Cleaner and better-liked than SignUpGenius on Capterra/G2 — reviewers praise ease of use, reminders, and that participants don't need accounts. Weakness is the same one: ads on the free tier, and reviewers specifically say the ad-free upgrade is 'too expensive for small group quarterly signups.'

competitors.name: Google Forms + Google Sheets
competitors.note: The real competitor for anyone technical enough. Fatal flaw everyone hits: Forms has no built-in per-option response limit and respondents cannot see what others already picked, so slots get double-booked and the organizer reconciles by hand in Sheets. Requires third-party add-ons (Choice Eliminator, Form Choice Limiter) to fix. Sharing the raw Sheet instead means volunteers overwrite or delete each other's rows.

competitors.name: A printed paper sheet / Word-PDF template
competitors.note: Still the actual incumbent in church foyers, breakrooms, and school back-to-school nights — template.net, eForms, and Spreadsheet123 all rank for it. Wins on zero friction and zero trust barrier; loses because remote people can't see it, it gets lost, and the organizer retypes it. Any app here must be printable to compete with it rather than against it.

competitors.name: PerfectPotluck
competitors.note: Single-purpose potluck tool with a long tail of loyal users. Roundups consistently ding it for dated design and ads. Proof that a narrow, no-account tool survives in this niche on habit alone.

competitors.name: Doodle
competitors.model: Freemium. Poll creation now requires an account; free tier shows ads; 'if need be' vote, reminders and deadlines are paywalled. Pro ~$6.95/mo.
competitors.note: Adjacent (time polling, not slot claiming) but the most instructive cautionary tale: it ratcheted from free-and-account-free to account-required-plus-ads-plus-paywalled-core-feature over several years. 'Doodle alternative' search volume has grown every year since 2020. This is exactly the arc our stance promises never to walk.

competitors.name: Evite SignUp Sheets
competitors.note: Ships the organizer-side basics we should match: CSV of all signups plus a printable version. Aesthetic is the reference point for 'dated' — reviewers describe Evite's templates as clip-art that hasn't changed in a decade.

competitors.name: Grasshopper Signup / SignUpReady / Serve.love
competitors.model: Free, ad-free, no-account (claimed). Venture-less indie insurgents.
competitors.note: A whole cohort launched in 2024-2026 explicitly positioned as 'the ad-free SignUpGenius.' They validate our thesis and they are our nearest competition — but all are hosted web services with accounts and databases, so they can still ad-ify or paywall later. Our static, offline, nothing-leaves-the-device build is a claim they structurally cannot make.

complaints.complaint: "People have to endure SO MANY ads to sign up. I'm considering moving away from Sign Up Genius simply because of that." Ads on the free tier are the #1 complaint, and they land on the *participant*, not the organizer — the organizer's neighbors and fellow parents are the ones getting the video ads.
complaints.source: SignUpReady roundup of SignUpGenius ad complaints; corroborated by Capterra reviews ("There are a lot of ads on the screen that can sometimes get in the way") and Apple App Store reviews
complaints.weWinIf: Zero ads, ever, and we say so *on the shared sheet itself* — a quiet footer line the organizer's invitees can see: "No ads. No account. No email required." The organizer is sending this link to people whose opinion of them matters; make the sheet a thing they're proud to send.

complaints.complaint: Pop-up ads land on top of the claim buttons, and video ads reset scroll position mid-page, forcing people to restart the signup. "The app serves me one useless ad after another and reopens the same ad multiple times after I've closed it."
complaints.source: Apple App Store 1-star reviews for SignUpGenius iOS (app rated 1.2 / 5 from 125 ratings)
complaints.weWinIf: Nothing ever moves after first paint. No layout shift, no interstitial, no cookie banner (we set no cookies), no 'install our app' bar. The claim button is where it was 200ms ago.

complaints.complaint: Race condition on claiming: "by the time I have gotten to the end, another person has taken that spot" — and the typed name is lost, so the whole flow restarts.
complaints.weWinIf: Claim optimistically and never discard typed input. If the slot fills underneath them, keep the name in the field, say plainly what happened, and offer the nearest still-open slot as a single tap. This is a small amount of code that fixes the most humiliating moment in the category.

complaints.complaint: Mobile rendering is a shrunken desktop view: "the actual signup on the phone screen displays way too much information... everything is too small as if you're on the desktop version," requiring pinch-zoom to read slot rows.
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews and mobile complaints surfaced in search of SignUpGenius mobile experience
complaints.weWinIf: Design the participant view mobile-first as a vertical list of cards, never a horizontal grid. Minimum 17px body, 44-56px tap targets, no horizontal scroll at 320px. The grid layout is a desktop artifact; participants are almost always on a phone.

complaints.complaint: "The layout often times may get a little annoying when scrolling down to find open time slots" — on a long sheet you cannot tell what is still available without scrolling the entire thing.
complaints.weWinIf: A persistent 'still needed' summary at the top, written as a sentence a human would say: "Still needed: 2 desserts, 1 salad, and someone to bring ice." Plus a one-tap 'show only open slots' filter. Availability should be answerable in under two seconds without scrolling.

complaints.complaint: Setup is unintuitive: "The features and directions are not very clearly described," users trial-and-error their way through timeblocks, and creation requires navigating multiple steps. Long-time organizers say it "was a pain to set up."
complaints.source: Capterra SignUpGenius reviews; Grasshopper/Serve.love comparison pages citing switchers
complaints.weWinIf: Sheet creation must be under 60 seconds with no wizard. One screen: title, date, and a fast repeating-row editor. Ship presets (potluck by course, 2-hour shift blocks, 10-minute conference slots, meal train by date) so the common case is two taps, not twelve fields.

complaints.complaint: Email overhead in both directions: participants get promotional messages they didn't ask for, confirmations land in spam, and SignUpGenius itself concedes "occasionally email providers completely block a reminder because they think it's spam." There are 12 registered spam complaints against the domain.
complaints.source: SignUpGenius support docs on reminder deliverability; Spam.org domain complaint registry; Capterra notes on email/notification issues
complaints.weWinIf: Don't collect email at all. Replace the reminder email with an .ics calendar file generated on-device the moment they claim a slot — the commitment lands in the calendar they already check, with no deliverability risk and no address harvested. Frame it as a feature, not a limitation.

complaints.complaint: Privacy language that doesn't actually promise anything: SignUpGenius says it does not sell information "purely for profit, to data brokers, or in any way other than those intended to improve online experiences and the relevance of offers" — a carve-out big enough to drive ad targeting through.
complaints.weWinIf: A one-sentence privacy claim with no subordinate clause, verifiable by anyone: the sheet lives on your device; we have no server that could receive your name. Link the source. This is the one claim in the category nobody funded can copy.

complaints.complaint: "Their user experience is deeply flawed" and the interface changes often enough that people can't relocate features; 15-year users report the product has "deteriorated significantly" and are actively leaving.
complaints.source: Apple App Store 1-star reviews for SignUpGenius
complaints.weWinIf: Stability as a promise. Never move the claim button between releases. Ship a visible, dated changelog so a returning organizer knows nothing they learned has been invalidated.

complaints.complaint: Interface is "dated, cluttered, and visually unappealing... distracting ads, loud graphics, and a lack of modern design elements," and one reviewer says outright: "I think the layout needs a makeover to keep up with the aesthetic expectations." The ads make the page "look less legit."
complaints.source: Capterra SignUpGenius reviews; SoftwareAdvice profile; Grasshopper/Serve.love comparison writeups
complaints.weWinIf: Look credible enough that a stranger trusts an unsolicited link. That means restraint, not decoration: generous whitespace, one accent color, real typographic hierarchy, and a visible organizer name and event date above the fold so it reads as a real invitation rather than a phishing page.

complaints.complaint: Sheets are write-once graveyards — "unused slots don't auto-delete after event dates pass" and organizers can't find their old sign-ups without an account.
complaints.weWinIf: A local 'my sheets' list on the organizer's device with past events collapsed automatically, plus one-tap 'duplicate for next month.' Recurring coordination (meal trains, monthly snack rotas, weekly nursery shifts) is the real usage pattern and nobody serves it well.

complaints.complaint: Google Forms fails at the one job: "respondents can't see what others have selected" and there's no per-option limit, so time slots get overbooked and the organizer reconciles by hand. Sharing the Sheet directly instead means volunteers "delete entries, alter existing data, or corrupt the document's structure."
complaints.source: Formester and Qualtir guides on Google Forms response limits; Everest Web Deals Choice Eliminator docs; CivicChamps guide on Google volunteer sheets
complaints.weWinIf: Show taken slots with the claimer's name visible by default — that IS the product. Social proof drives signups (people join when they see neighbors already in), and visible capacity is the entire reason to not use a Google Form. Never make the participant guess what's left.

tableStakes: Live availability visible without scrolling — a per-slot 'x of y spots left' and a total-remaining summary at the top. Its absence is exactly why Google Forms loses this category.
Taken slots show WHO took them, by name, by default. This is social proof and it measurably drives signups; hiding it makes the sheet feel dead.
Claim a slot with no account, no email, no verification step — name field plus one tap. Participants must never hit a signup wall to sign up.
Un-claim or edit your own entry from the same link with no login, days later, on the same device. Every credible tool has an 'already signed up? change it' path.
Slots that need more than one person, and items that need a quantity ('bring 2 dozen cookies', '3 volunteers needed'). One-person-per-row is a toy.
A notes/comment field per claim — 'I'll bring the gluten-free one', 'arriving 15 min late', dietary flags. Organizers depend on this and it costs nothing.
Multi-slot claiming with a configurable cap ('you may take up to 2'), so one eager parent doesn't silently take everything.
Share surface beyond the raw URL: a QR code for the bulletin board or flyer, and a copy-as-plain-text block for pasting into a group text, WhatsApp, or Remind.
An organizer view that exports — CSV plus a printer-friendly one-page check-in sheet to carry to the event. Evite, Grasshopper, and Jotform all ship this; its absence reads as unfinished.

Some form of commitment reminder. Everyone else sends reminder emails; without a backend, an .ics calendar download at the moment of claiming is the credible client-side equivalent — but shipping nothing here would be the most visible gap in the app.
differentiators: Put the stance on the participant-facing sheet, not just the marketing page. A quiet footer line on every shared sheet: 'No ads. No account. No email collected.' The competitive fact behind it is brutal — SignUpGenius Silver is $11.99/mo and buys exactly ONE ad-free sign up. Organizers are sending this link to their neighbors; make it something they're proud to send.

Copy-as-text share block. Render the whole sheet as clean plain text with the link at the bottom, formatted to paste straight into a group chat, WhatsApp, Remind, or a church bulletin. This is how these links actually spread and nobody does it well. Pure client-side, an afternoon of work.

.ics download the instant someone claims a slot. It is our answer to reminder emails, and it is arguably better: it lands in the calendar they already check, can't be blocked as spam, and requires harvesting no email address. Reframe the constraint as the feature.

A print mode that looks like a real sign-up sheet — one page, large rows, the claimed names filled in, and blank lines at the bottom for walk-ups. We are competing with paper on the church foyer table; the winning move is to be printable to paper rather than to fight it.

Never lose typed input on a claim collision. If a slot fills while someone is typing, keep their name, explain it in one plain sentence, and offer the nearest open slot as a single tap. This directly fixes the most-cited indignity in the category's reviews.

No-account organizer ownership done honestly: an edit key held on the organizer's device, plus a copyable/printable 'organizer link' they can save to email themselves. Be explicit about the tradeoff up front ('save this link — it's the only way back in') rather than discovering it as a bug later.

'Duplicate for next time' on any past sheet, with a local list of your sheets and past events auto-collapsed. Meal trains, monthly snack rotas, and weekly nursery shifts are the real recurring pattern and the incumbents leave old sheets to rot.

Presets tuned to the four real occasions rather than one generic builder: potluck by course, shift blocks by time, conference/parent-teacher 10-minute slots, and a meal train by date. Sensible defaults per preset (a meal train defaults to one household per day, with allergy notes on by default) make the 60-second setup real.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The category is visually stuck. SignUpGenius is repeatedly described in its own reviews as 'dated, cluttered, and visually unappealing... distracting ads, loud graphics, and a lack of modern design elements,' with one reviewer asking outright for a makeover 'to keep up with the aesthetic expectations.' Evite's templates are described as clip-art that 'hasn't changed much in the last decade.' PerfectPotluck is dinged for the same. The house style across the incumbents is: a dense horizontal table of date/slot/name columns, decorative clip-art 'themes' (balloons, chalkboards, autumn leaves) chosen by the organizer, saturated primary colors, small type, and an ad rail. What reads as CURRENT in 2026 is the opposite of every one of those: vertical card lists instead of tables, one restrained accent color instead of theme skins, real typographic hierarchy carrying the structure, generous whitespace, and legible-at-arm's-length type. Partiful shows what modern looks like in the adjacent invite space — mobile-first, opinionated, shareable — but it is deliberately loud and 'unserious,' and copying its energy would be a serious misread here (see emotional context). The correct read is Partiful's craft standard with a completely different temperature. Concretely dated: multi-column slot grids on mobile, decorative theme wallpapers, drop shadows on everything, gradient buttons, clip-art icons, anything that needs pinch-zoom.
aesthetic.emotionalContext:
There are two users in genuinely different states, and the volume user is the one everyone designs for last.

The PARTICIPANT (95% of sessions): got a link in a group text or a forwarded email. They are one-handed on a phone, standing in a school pickup line, on the couch half-watching TV, or walking. Attention window is roughly fifteen seconds and the alternative to completing is closing the tab and feeling vaguely guilty. They need three things in this order: what's left, can I do one of them, done. They arrive with mild suspicion — an unsolicited link — so the page has about one second to look legitimate rather than like phishing. Design consequences: 17px minimum body text, 44-56px tap targets, thumb-reachable claim action, no horizontal scroll at 320px, high contrast for outdoor daylight readability, and zero layout shift after first paint.

The ORGANIZER (5% of sessions, 100% of the decision to adopt): a room parent, PTA volunteer coordinator, deacon, office admin, or conference track chair doing unpaid coordination labor at 9:30pm after the kids are down, or in the ten minutes between meetings. They are time-poor and mildly resentful of the task. They have been burned before — by the sheet nobody filled, by the ads that made them look unprofessional to their neighbors, by the parent who couldn't figure it out and texted them at 10pm. They need to build and send in under a minute and to trust that the link will not embarrass them.

The part almost everyone gets wrong: this tool is not only used for parties. The same sheet format runs meal trains for a family after a death or a cancer diagnosis, hospice volunteer shifts, and funeral reception food. A playful, confetti, party-energy aesthetic is actively wrong in those moments and will read as callous. The design must be warm enough for a class potluck and dignified enough for a bereavement meal train, without changing skins.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: Warm, hospitable, calm, legible, dignified, unfussy

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Deep warm amber / honey — a burnt-honey primary around #B45309 to #C2700A for actions, with a soft amber wash (#FEF3E2 / #FDEBD0) for claimed and highlighted surfaces, on a warm off-white paper ground (#FDFBF7) with warm near-black ink (#2A2118) rather than pure black. Secondary supporting hue: a muted sage or moss (#5F7355) for 'filled / complete' states so the success signal doesn't collide with the primary.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Amber is the color of lamplight, a shared table, a casserole dish, a church-basement kitchen. It carries the exact emotion of this act — communal hospitality, mild obligation, warmth extended to a group — without becoming celebratory. Critically, it holds both ends of the use range: it is welcoming enough for a class potluck and quiet enough for a bereavement meal train, which a party palette cannot do. It also solves the differentiation problem: the category is owned by SignUpGenius green, Doodle/Evite blue, and SignUp.com's brighter corporate orange, so a deeper, desaturated burnt-honey is recognizably not any of them while staying in the warm family that fits the emotion. Within a 23-app portfolio it occupies a hue band that utility apps rarely claim. Execution note that matters: do NOT use amber as button fill with white text at light values — it fails contrast. Use the deep #B45309 end for the primary button (passes 4.5:1 on white), reserve the light amber wash for surfaces and 'you claimed this' states, and let the warm near-black ink carry all body text. Print mode should collapse to ink-on-paper cleanly, since organizers will print it. If amber is already claimed elsewhere in the portfolio, the next-best fit is a deep mulberry/plum (#7A3B5C range) — same warmth, same dignity, equally uncommon in this category.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Avoid SaaS blue (#2563EB and neighbors) — it is what Doodle and Evite already look like, it reads generic-corporate, and it is the single most over-claimed hue in any app portfolio. Avoid the SignUpGenius green: it is the category cliché and, worse, it makes us look like the thing we are replacing. Avoid party/celebration signals entirely — confetti, gradients, balloon or clip-art iconography, neon or Partiful-style high-energy palettes — because the same sheet gets used for funeral receptions and hospice shifts and that misread is unforgivable. Avoid pastel millennial peach/mint: low contrast in daylight (this is used outdoors in a pickup line) and it reads unserious. Avoid pure black on pure white — too cold against a warm accent and unnecessarily harsh. Avoid any organizer-selectable decorative 'theme' system at all; the incumbents' theme skins are precisely what makes their pages look dated and untrustworthy.

confidence: Medium-high on the competitive and complaint picture; medium on a few specific numbers. What is well-corroborated across independent sources: ads as the dominant complaint (Capterra cons, Apple App Store reviews, and multiple roundups agree); the Google Forms availability/limit failure (documented in Google Forms guides and by the existence of Choice Eliminator add-ons); Doodle's ratchet from free to account-required-plus-ads-plus-paywalled-features; and the 'dated interface' consensus (Capterra, SoftwareAdvice, multiple roundups). WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, and you should treat with care: (1) The SignUpGenius iOS rating of 1.2 stars from 125 ratings came from two fetches of the Apple App Store listing and the review text is consistent with it, but a 1.2 average is unusually low and worth a manual eyeball before quoting it publicly. (2) I could NOT reach Reddit directly — the site:reddit.com operator returned no usable threads and Trustpilot returned 403. Every 'Reddit says' claim here is secondhand via competitor roundups; I have attributed them accordingly and have not invented any Reddit quote. (3) A large share of the 'best X 2026' and 'alternatives' pages that rank for these queries are content marketing published BY competitors (signupready.com, grasshoppersignup.com, serve.love, getzelos.com, syncwhen.com, usecarly.com). Their factual claims about rivals' prices and ad behavior are directionally corroborated by Capterra and the App Store, but their comparative framing is not independent and I would not cite them as neutral. (4) SignUpGenius pricing ($11.99/$29.99/$59.99 monthly; Silver = 1 ad-free sign up) came from Capterra and aggregator pages, not the vendor's own pricing page, which I could not parse — verify before putting exact dollar figures in any public copy. (5) Competitor brand colors are from my own knowledge, not verified in this session; the differentiation argument holds regardless, but don't quote hex values for their brands. (6) I found no direct evidence on how organizers currently handle the meal-train / bereavement use case; that read is inference from the category's usage breadth, and it is the assumption I would most want validated with a few real user conversations before it drives the whole visual direction.
